place-work.text: Copying, painting, teaching, administration and water maintenance were different tasks. Manuscript study and endowed-property records expose some of their organization without identifying every workshop, laborer or household’s access.

patronage.text: Book copying and illustration, commercial buildings and religious foundations reveal different makers and patrons in an active urban setting.

inequality.text: An illustrated book made for an Uzbek patron gives privileged access to a cultivated elite’s representation; it does not speak equally for all urban residents.

evidence.text: Copying, painting and literary composition belong to separate moments; place attribution remains qualified.

name: Bukhara: books, markets and water
geographicPrecision: Urban locator; the manuscript is probably attributed to Bukhara, not securely documented at a named workshop. No khanate borders are reconstructed.

interval.label: Selected Shaibanid and Janid urban contexts, c. 1500–1785
interval.note: Investigation spans the two periods described in the archaeological source, not the founding or end of Bukhara. Individual buildings and manuscript stages have their own dates.

question: What changes when a book, a market and a reservoir are read together?
summary: A painted book, restored teaching spaces and water infrastructure reveal work behind an urban setting. Copyists, painters, teachers, administrators and people sustaining water systems appear through different sources, with unequal visibility and distinct dates.

sections.title: A book made through several acts
sections.text: This folio joins writing, painted figures, patterned surfaces and gold on paper. The Met attributes its painting to Shaikh Zada. The manuscript was likely copied in Herat, then illustrated for an Uzbek patron, probably in Bukhara in the 1530s. Sa‘di’s poem, completed in 1257, was older than both acts. Words had to be copied and a painted scene arranged on a bounded page. Those tasks did not happen at the poem’s composition. The reception gives selected forms of luxury a place within a literary image; it does not supply a survey of ordinary homes.

sections.title: Skills moved, and workshops organized work
sections.text: Comstock-Skipp describes invited and captured artists contributing to manuscripts in sixteenth-century Bukhara. Movement could involve coercion as well as opportunity. She interprets repeated figures and compositions in later books as evidence of organized production, challenging the assumption that repetition simply means inferior art. A general material account adds practical tasks: smoothing paper and preparing pigment with a binder precede controlled brushwork. These help explain skilled making without identifying this folio’s complete staff, exact pigments or workshop recipe.

sections.title: Teaching used rooms that needed care
sections.text: Learning also depended on built places. The architectural account describes the older Ulugh Beg madrasa with a courtyard, cells, a classroom and a mosque. Built in 1417, it was restored in 1585. Learning and prayer thus depended on physical spaces within an institution whose fabric could be repaired. Mir-i Arab, dated 1535–36, added another foundation to the city. These descriptions make education more concrete than a list of famous monuments, while leaving daily timetables and the experience of particular students unresolved.

citations.locator: Ulugh Beg madrasa layout and restoration; Mir-i Arab construction

sections.title: Water and income sustained institutions
sections.text: Canals supplied fields, while drainage carried away runoff and helped manage salts. McChesney explains why construction, maintenance and investment mattered, with Bukhara examples in a wider regional account. Urban reservoirs belonged to this work of provision: the Lab-i Hauz complex brought a reservoir together with a madrasa and khanaqah in 1619–23. Endowed property supplied income for institutions and their employees. The wealthy Juybari family sponsored repairs, canals and learning foundations while also preserving family influence. Books and buildings therefore lead to people managing resources, not only the patrons whose names survive.

deeperReading.title: A foundation had records as well as walls
deeperReading.text: McChesney distinguishes purchase records, endowment deeds and biographies favorable to the Juybari family. They do different work as evidence. Property income could support public institutions, while establishing an endowment also helped perpetuate the family. His account of administrative roles includes scribes and supervision of household and workshop accounts. Such records bring calculation and supervision into view alongside monumental patronage. They do not make every employee’s voice equally audible. A biography praising its patron and a deed defining resources should not be treated as interchangeable descriptions of a shared experience. Here the original manuscripts and deeds remain unread; the explanation uses the historian’s selected analysis.

citations.locator: Source discussion; administration; Monuments and public works

deeperReading.title: Maintenance also raises a question about power
deeperReading.text: A canal was not useful simply because someone once ordered it built. Continued water flow depended on maintenance and resources, and land value varied with access to the system. This practical relationship linked fields, food and urban institutions. It could also create unequal obligations. McChesney describes requisitioned labor in a large project in the Vakhsh basin. That example belongs to another location; it is not a recovered crew for Bukhara’s reservoir. It does show why useful infrastructure should not automatically be called voluntary cooperation. The present sources explain investment and institutional support more clearly than household water rights, everyday cleaning routines or the conditions of particular workers.

evidenceReading.title: A page, a building description and an institutional record
evidenceReading.introduction: These are modern paraphrases of selected sources, not translations of inscriptions, manuscript text or endowment deeds.

items.label: The selected folio and its catalogue
items.text: The catalogue distinguishes an older poem, likely copying in Herat and later painting probably in Bukhara. The visible page brings writing, figures and patterned surfaces into one composition.
items.interpretation: An image can support observations about represented goods and artistic choices. Its architecture is not a measured Bukharan house or madrasa, and its reception is not evidence of every household’s experience.

items.label: Restoration is a dated activity
items.text: The architectural account gives 1417 for the Ulugh Beg madrasa’s construction and 1585 for restoration, alongside a description of its courtyard, cells, classroom and mosque.
items.interpretation: A building can combine older design with later care. The restoration date does not date every surviving component or prove an unchanged curriculum. This is evidence of an institution continuing through work on material fabric.

items.label: Resources supported people as well as structures
items.text: McChesney’s endowment analysis connects property income with institutional functions and employees, while also identifying the family’s interests in preserving its position.
items.interpretation: Funding helps explain how a foundation could continue after its construction. The selected analysis does not establish equal benefit or reveal every obligation; it should be compared with household and worker testimony when such evidence becomes available.

review.scope: Selected museum catalogue, architectural synthesis, manuscript scholarship and institutional/economic analysis. Original case dates, claims, object order, full media metadata and image bytes are retained.
limitations: No complete original endowment deed, manuscript biography, workshop account or cited architectural monograph freshly read. Selected claims mediated through named modern scholars remain attributed.
The folio’s likely copying and probable painting place remain qualified; its depicted architecture is not a recovered school, workshop, home or water system.

Household water rights, particular maintenance routines, exact working conditions and the experience of students and workers remain incompletely documented here. The Vakhsh labor example is not relocated to Bukhara.

No new photograph, historical plan, route, border, numeric locator or source-derived diagram is added. Full family usability, screen-reader behavior, physical print and independent historical acceptance remain separate tasks.
